key_findings.finding: Extreme Greed sentiment yields the highest average PnL (205.82) despite having a lower win rate (55.3%) than Neutral (49.5%) and Greed (43.6%)
key_findings.why_it_matters: Suggests that high-conviction trades in extreme market conditions are more profitable on average, even if they are less frequently correct. Traders may benefit from focusing on high-conviction setups rather than optimizing for win rate alone.

key_findings.finding: Contrarian Winners have a lower win rate (26.1%) but higher average PnL (137.684) than Sentiment Followers (win rate: 43.4%, avg PnL: 62.001)
key_findings.why_it_matters: Contrarian strategies may sacrifice frequency for higher-magnitude gains, indicating that disciplined contrarian trading could be a viable edge in crypto markets where sentiment-driven moves are common.

key_findings.finding: Trade count is the third most important profitability driver (0.165) after avg PnL per size (0.272) and win rate (0.2513), but profitability is highly skewed (87.5% of traders are profitable)
key_findings.why_it_matters: Suggests that while volume matters, it is less critical than trade quality (size and win rate). The high profitability rate may indicate survivorship bias or that the dataset excludes unprofitable traders entirely.

key_findings.finding: Contrarian score is higher for profitable traders (0.57) than unprofitable ones (0.365), but Contrarian Winners have lower trader consistency (0.018) than Sentiment Followers (0.097)
key_findings.why_it_matters: Contrarian strategies require high discipline to execute consistently, but when executed well, they outperform. Low consistency may explain why many contrarians fail, despite the strategy's potential.

contradictions: Extreme Greed sentiment has the highest avg PnL but the lowest trade count (5621), while Fear has the highest trade count (13869) but lower avg PnL (128.29). This suggests that extreme sentiment conditions are rare but highly profitable when they occur.

Contrarian Winners have a much lower win rate (26.1%) than Sentiment Followers (43.4%), yet they achieve higher avg PnL (137.684 vs. 62.001). This contradicts the common assumption that higher win rates always lead to better profitability.
Top 10% traders have a win rate of 46.1%, which is only marginally better than the overall dataset's win rate implied by 87.5% profitability (likely skewed by small sample size of 32 traders).
recommended_next_analyses: Analyze the distribution of trade sizes to determine if Extreme Greed trades are concentrated in a few large positions, explaining the high avg PnL despite low win rate.
Examine the correlation between contrarian score and PnL across different market regimes (e.g., bull vs. bear markets) to validate if contrarian strategies are regime-dependent.
Investigate the survivorship bias in the dataset by comparing the performance of traders who exited the dataset vs. those who remained, to assess the true profitability distribution.
Run a cluster analysis on trader archetypes to identify if there are hidden sub-groups within 'Contrarian Winners' or 'Sentiment Followers' that exhibit different performance characteristics.
Compare the avg PnL per size and win rate of top vs. bottom traders to determine if the top performers are simply trading larger positions or if they have a genuine edge in trade selection.
overall_summary: The data reveals that high-conviction and contrarian strategies outperform sentiment-following approaches, despite lower win rates. However, the extreme skewness in profitability (87.5% profitable traders) and low sample size (32 traders) suggest potential survivorship bias. Contrarian strategies require high discipline but can yield outsized returns when executed correctly.
